## Categories do more than describe {.statement}

They tell people what differences are expected to matter.

## The puzzle {.question}

Why do tidy classifications produce untidy decisions?

## Three operations

Every working classification must:

1. **Draw a boundary** around an object.
2. **Name a difference** inside that boundary.
3. **Attach a consequence** to the name.

## The category is not the case {.quote}

> A label compresses a history. It does not replace one.

::: {.quote-source}
Original text written for this synthetic example
:::

# The consequence of compression

## Compression creates leverage {.statement}

The same simplification that enables coordination can conceal disagreement.

## Ask where revision is possible {.question}

Who may challenge the boundary, the name, or the consequence?

## A better ending

Do not ask whether a category is perfectly true.

Ask whether it is:

- clear enough to coordinate action;
- open enough to absorb exceptions;
- revisable by the people it affects.

## Keep the map corrigible {.statement}

Useful classifications leave a visible route for correction.
